vignette:
He is an 80-year-old man from Southeast Asia, widowed now for many years, who still introduces himself first through his work. Even in retirement, he says he is "a data scientist," with the same small, apologetic smile, as if the title explains why he notices patterns in everything and why some memories have never loosened their grip. When he begins talking about the war, he does not start with fear. He starts with logistics.

As a young man, he is trained in mathematics and statistics and recruited into relief work because he can organize supply records, track displaced families, and make sense of chaotic numbers when others are overwhelmed. He is sent into a war zone where camps swell overnight, roads vanish under shelling, and every list is outdated by morning. At first he believes that careful counting can save people. He spends long days under canvas roofs, entering names by hand, estimating food needs, matching scarce medicine to impossible demand. He tells himself that if the numbers are accurate, fewer people will die.

Then the violence comes closer. One afternoon, while he is helping unload sacks of rice and tins of powdered milk near a crowded distribution site, incoming fire lands nearby. He remembers the sound first-a cracking roar, then a pressure that seems to punch the air out of his chest. Dust and metal scatter. People run in every direction. He drops to the ground and sees, with terrible clarity, one of the local drivers lying twisted beside an overturned truck. He can smell diesel, blood, and hot earth. A child is screaming for her mother. Someone grabs his shirt and shouts at him to move, but for a moment he cannot. Later he is ashamed of that frozen moment and returns to it often, as if there had been a correct mathematical solution to panic and he failed to find it.

After that day, the work continues because it has to. He helps carry the injured. He updates casualty sheets. He sleeps lightly, boots on, listening for engines and artillery. He learns to scan every field, every roadside ditch, every rooftop. He stops sitting with his back to open space. He does not tell anyone that his hands shake when he writes. At night, when he does sleep, he wakes convinced that he hears the same impact again. He begins to dread the distribution lines, not only because they are targets but because the pleading faces of civilians force him to choose who receives too little. He survives by becoming more precise, more controlled, more devoted to his ledgers.

Years later, after resettling and building a career in data science, he appears successful and disciplined. He marries, raises a family, becomes known as the quiet man who is never late and never wastes words. In professional settings he is respected for his ability to detect anomalies in vast systems. He likes the cleanliness of code, the reassurance of models that behave as expected. Yet his colleagues do not see how much of his orderliness is built around fear. He keeps multiple backup plans, memorizes exits in every building, and grows tense when meetings become crowded or noisy. Sudden bangs-a dropped metal cart, construction outside the office, fireworks during holidays-jolt him upright before he can think. For a second he is no longer in a conference room but back in dust and heat, waiting for another blast.

His wife understands more than anyone, though even with her he says little. She notices that he patrols the house at night, checking locks twice, then again. She learns not to wake him abruptly because he sometimes comes up swinging, disoriented and terrified. On some mornings she finds him already dressed before dawn, sitting rigid at the kitchen table, staring into tea gone cold. After she dies, the house becomes unbearably silent. Without her steady presence, the nights lengthen. He sleeps in fragments. He avoids the news but is drawn to headlines about displacement and war, then feels sick and guilty for reading them. Images of refugees waiting for aid can ruin the rest of his day. He tells himself he should have done more, sent more, stayed longer, saved someone he cannot name.

Now, at 80, he still spends hours at his computer analyzing public datasets and volunteering remotely on humanitarian forecasting projects. He says it keeps his mind active, but it also keeps him close to the old emergency in a way that both steadies and wounds him. He becomes irritated when routines are disrupted. He rarely attends community celebrations because crowds make him feel trapped. In restaurants he chooses the seat facing the door. He avoids talking about the war with his children because he does not want to "burden them," yet he feels alone with memories that arrive uninvited: the driver by the truck, the child screaming, the awful knowledge that after the shelling stopped there were still names to count.

He presents as composed, exact, and courteous, but beneath that restraint is a man who has spent decades living as though catastrophe might resume at any moment. He is tired of being startled by ordinary sounds, tired of nights broken by the same scenes, tired of measuring his life against those he could not protect. Even now, when he looks at a spreadsheet of human need, he feels the old urgency in his body before he feels it in his mind.
